sources.description: Project Drawdown's assessments of climate solutions at global scale. sources.description: Production, consumption, trade, reserves, capacity and CO2 emissions by country and fuel for 265 country, region and aggregate codes, in natural units, terawatt-hours and quadrillion Btu. Most series are annual, 1980 to 2024; a few are monthly (to May 2026 in the file of 3 October 2026). Primary-energy accounting: fossil fuels at their heat content; non-combustible renewable electricity (hydro, wind, solar, geothermal, tide) at the heat content of the electricity, 3,412 Btu per kWh (the captured-energy approach); nuclear at the heat input of nuclear plants. Checked in the file of 3 October 2026 for World 2024: wind 8.570 quad Btu from 2,511.7 billion kWh (3,412 Btu per kWh), hydro 3,412, nuclear 28.386 quad Btu from 2,735.1 billion kWh (10,379 Btu per kWh). This differs from the Energy Institute's physical-energy-content totals and from the older fossil-fuel-equivalent method, so series from different producers are never joined. World total energy consumption 2024 is 606.04 quad Btu; the by-fuel series sum to 607.48, and the gap is left as published.

citation.title: Quantifying the potential for climate change mitigation of consumption options

sources.description: A systematic review of 53 studies published after 2011, which found 771 consumption options and summarised them as 61 options in transport, housing, food and other consumption. For each option the paper reports the greenhouse gas mitigation potential in tonnes of CO2-equivalent per person per year: the mean, the median, the 25th and 75th percentiles and the range across studies. The paper's figures order options by median. The values come mostly from high-income settings, depend on context (grid mix, the car replaced, the starting diet) and are not additive. Footprint figures quoted for context (about 6 t per person worldwide, 13.4 t North America, 7.5 t Europe, 1.7 t Africa and Middle East) refer to 2011.
